grading.question: Why can k-fold cross-validation give a more reliable estimate of model performance than a single train/test split?

answers.text: A single split depends heavily on which rows land in the test set, so its estimate has high variance. K-fold rotates every row through the test fold and averages k scores, which lowers that variance and uses all the data for both training and evaluation. The trade-off is k times the training cost, and for time-series data the folds must keep time order to avoid leakage.
Because it tests the model more than once on different parts of the data and averages the results, so one lucky split matters less.

grading.question: A table of 50 million orders is queried by customer_id and created_at. Queries take 9 seconds and the plan shows a sequential scan. Diagnose the problem and say what you would change.

answers.text: The sequential scan means there is no usable index for the filter, so the database reads all 50 million rows. I would add a composite index on (customer_id, created_at) with the equality column first, so the planner can seek to one customer and range-scan by date. Then I would check the plan again with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. The trade-off is slower writes and extra storage for the index.

grading.question: You run a web server where a nightly batch job makes interactive requests slow. You cannot move the job to another machine. What would you do, and why?

answers.text: I would lower the batch job's priority with nice or a cgroup CPU limit so the scheduler favours the interactive request threads, and limit its I/O with ionice because batch jobs often starve the disk. If that is not enough I would split the job into smaller chunks with pauses. The trade-off is that the job runs longer, so I would check it still finishes before morning.
